content.value:
A flywheel is a spinning mass used to launch game pieces. The goal: spin a GoBILDA 6000 RPM motor at full speed and hold it.

Open FlywheelConfig.java. All tuning constants are defined here: motor type, target RPM, and PID/feedforward coefficients — all set to zero.

Flywheel.java reads from FlywheelConfig and uses voltage compensation: motor.set(14.0 / voltage) cancels battery sag so the flywheel runs the same speed regardless of battery level.

FlywheelTuningOpMode.java displays the target vs actual RPM in telemetry.

Use the Programming Board robot config for a single motor named "motor".

A config file is a single source of truth for your constants.

Instead of magic numbers scattered across your code — kP=0.15 in one file, target=6000 in another, motor type hidden in a constructor — you put everything in one place.

Benefits:

One place to tune — change a number in FlywheelConfig, rebuild, done.

No duplicates — if targetRPM is used in telemetry, calculations, and display, you reference the constant, not copy the number.

Self-documenting — someone reading FlywheelConfig immediately sees what's tunable and what hardware you're using.

Competition-ready — after tuning, hardcode your final values here and don't touch them again.

steps.title: Step 1: Find kS — overcome static friction

content.value:
kS is the minimum voltage needed to just barely start the motor spinning, in ticks per second.

The feedforward output is in ticks/sec and gets divided by the motor's max ticks/sec to become a power value. So kS = 0.1 contributes only 0.1/2800 = 0.000036 power — invisible.

In FlywheelConfig, keep kV, kP, kI, kD at 0.

Increase kS from 0. Start at 100. Increase in steps of 50. Rebuild each time.

Watch the RPM telemetry. Stop when the flywheel just barely starts to spin — RPM should be very low, 50-200.

Too high: the flywheel spins faster than needed from static friction alone.

Too low: the motor doesn't move at all.

steps.title: Step 2: Find kV — map velocity to power

content.value:
kV converts target velocity to feedforward output, in ticks per second per ticks/sec.

Keep your kS value. Keep PID at 0.

Increase kV. Start at 0.0001. Target velocity at full output is ~2800 ticks/sec, so kV × 2800 should give meaningful power.

With kV=0.00015: ff = kS + 0.00015 × 2800 = kS + 0.42. That's reasonable power.

If RPM is too low, increase kV. Too high, decrease kV.

Goal: feedforward alone (kS + kV, no PID) gets within ~500 RPM of target.

steps.title: Step 3: Tune kP — close the gap with PID

content.value:
Now add kP. Feedforward got you close; PID fine-tunes.

Start with kP = 0.001. Increase until RPM oscillates around the target, then back off.

The oscillation should stay within ~50 RPM of the target.

Good: RPM holds steady at target with minor correction.

Too high kP: wild swings, audible "hunting". Too low: drifts slowly.

Optionally add a tiny kD (0.0001) to dampen bounce and kI (0.00001) to eliminate steady offset. But kS + kV + kP alone should get you very close.

The tuning order matters:

kS first: without breaking friction, nothing else works.

kV second: feedforward handles most of the work, so PID's job is small.

kP last: PID fills the remaining gap.

Your FlywheelConfig now holds the correct constants. In a real robot, you'd tune once, save these values, and never touch them again.

The periodic() method uses motor.set(14.0 / voltage) to compensate for battery sag — the same formula from the voltage compensation lesson. Feedforward handles known physics, voltage compensation handles battery drain, PID handles the rest.
